text: — Well, wait, let me tell you how we went with Bay Ganyo to the exhibition in Prague — Tsvyatko said with a smile.
— Bravo, Tsvyatko! — we all shouted. — How long we've been waiting for this!
Tsvyatko began:

— If you remember, we set off from Sofia with a whole train of our own carriages and our own locomotive. Carriages of only the 1st and 2nd class, brand-new, having just arrived from Europe, impeccably clean and comfortable. In the very same carriage, there were both 1st and 2nd class compartments. A crowd of people — whether there were 160 of us, I don't remember. Old, young, women, men, children, and even infants. (Oh, those infants!...)

Who is like us! What pride it was that we were setting off for the exhibition with our own train. Let the Europeans see, we told ourselves, that Bulgaria is not asleep. But most of all, we puffed ourselves up with the novelty, the modern construction, and the cleanliness of the carriages. But for how long, do you think, did we enjoy the patriotic charm of the superiority of our carriages and the thought that we would stun Europe with our progress? While they were seeing us off at the station, while we were passing the Slivnitsa and Dragoman positions—the fields of our glorious victories—our enthusiasm grew proportionally with the emptying of the bottles and the baskets of provisions with which the practical tourists had abundantly supplied themselves. “Of course, we’ll take snacks; why should we give our money to the Serbs?” shouted Bay Ganyo, inspired by patriotism and Pleven wine. But as we approached Tsaribrod and it began to grow dark, when they tried to light the carriages and it turned out they had forgotten to prepare the lamps, when it became completely dark, when the children began to get scared and wail—oh, then little by little, as if with the slipping away of Bulgarian territory, our patriotic enthusiasm was also slipping away. Some smiled sadly, others smiled with hidden sarcasm (we were not only Bulgarians), others were indignant; even Bay Ganyo whispered in my ear: “Does a pig understand well water!” Some, on the other hand, let out unambiguous curses addressed to a foreigner serving in the management of our railways. Supported by the latter, Bay Ganyo cried out: “Don’t I know that we are not to blame, it’s those foreigners again, the devil take them! They did it on purpose to disgrace us! And do you realize, it’s all out of envy! They are all like that!”

At these words, he gave one of the foreigners such a look that it made him cough and move to the other compartment. When we stopped at the station in Tsaribrod, it was pitch black in the carriages; we couldn't even see one another. We got agitated, we got cross, and then we turned it into a joke. A host of jokes and barbs were launched at the expense of our railway officials. Shouts were heard: "Give us some candles, people, the children are frightened!", "Hey, uncle, go buy us a pound of candles, we'll give you a tip!", "Come on, at least give us one tallow candle each!" Only Bay Ganyo would not entertain the possibility that Bulgarians could be responsible for such mismanagement.

— That fellow over there, do you see him — he was saying, after they brought several simple candles, and he pointed at one of our "foreigners," — you should douse him in tar and set him on fire. Is this to be endured, man! Never mind the darkness, who cares about that — but we’ve become a disgrace before the Serbs. There he is, do you see him, a Serbian official — the man is laughing. He’s laughing, of course! But his aroused patriotism would not allow Bay Ganyo to tolerate a Serb smirking at him, so he frowned back at him:
— And why are you laughing there, hey! And he wanted to jump off the carriage and go settle things with the Serb. Heroic blood!
— Shh... Stand still, Bay Ganyo — the passengers were urging him — don't make a scene. Keep in mind that you are entering Serbia...
— Well, so what if I'm entering Serbia! Are they going to scare me? What about Slivnitsa? What about "back, brothers"—and from Bay Ganyo’s mouth a curse flew out like a bomb.
— How is the Serb to blame that our carriages were dark! — the others were calming him down.
— Who? Him? I know their kind! — replies Bay Ganyo and shakes his head.

They handed out one candle per compartment. Some lamps, I think, they managed to adjust and light. The train set off. The passengers dripped hot tallow on the windows and fixed the candles. This was the first   B u l g a r i a n i z a t i o n   of the new carriages. The second Bulgarianization took place during the very first night: all the toilets (excuse me, gentlemen) turned into cesspools.

Anyway, we passed through Serbia. But don't think that we passed through it just like that, quietly and modestly. Oho! The Bulgarian is no fool! Wherever there was an opportunity, Bay Ganyo did not miss a chance to sting the Serbs, to remind them of Slivnitsa. In Niš and Belgrade, he even asked all the officials and porters: "Aren't you a Bulgarian, tell the truth? You are all Bulgarians, but you're acting like Serbs."

We set off across Hungary!... Here, the wheels of one carriage caught fire! To hell with you and your craftsmen! We stopped for a long time. They poured water, extinguished, lit, smoldered... finally we set off. And the Magyars — laughter! They knew! — Bulgarian tourists!... And at one more place this carriage caught fire — finally they left it to the devil for repairs.

Bay Ganyo, an experienced man who had traveled before, was telling his simpler companions: — Now we're heading for Pest. Once we pass Pest — Vienna; Prague is beyond Vienna. I've scoured all these places — I know them like the back of my hand.

We did not stop at the small stations. At the large ones we stopped only long enough for them to clear the line. Wealthy Moravia caught everyone’s attention. The beautifully cultivated valleys, the magnificent gardens, the countless factories and plants made even Bay Ganyo admit Moravia’s superiority over our fatherland: “We work too, but these fellows don’t fall behind either, ah, they don’t fall behind, they know their business, these fellows.” But realizing he had gotten carried away with the praise, he added: “But it’s all for nothing. They work, and the German eats it.”

The journey did not pass without comedies. We—I, Vancho, Philyo, and Ivanitso’s son (I don’t believe you know him)—occupied a first-class compartment; in the neighboring, second-class section, Bai Ganyo settled in with several companions, richly supplied with provisions. Bai Ganyo, in his haste, it seemed, had forgotten to put any food in his saddlebags. “Well, after all, we are Bulgarians, we’ll look after one another. A piece of bread from this one, a bit of cheese from that one—a man will get by. Why not!” And indeed, he got by quite well. His companions treated him to food and drink—he treated them to the most fervent patriotism, mixed with appetite and thirst. But everything has an end. At last, our neighbors’ provisions ran out, and the flagons were emptied. (To avoid a gross error, I must correct myself: the flagons were emptied while we were still flying past Slivnitsa and Dragoman with “Long live Bulgaria, hurrah! Let me wet my whistle, man, hurrah!”)

Bay Ganyo began to sidle up to our compartment. At first he sought various pretexts: now he would ask for matches, now for a glass of cognac — because his stomach hurt — and then little by little he made himself at home, got used to it and, so to speak, would not leave our little room. He forgot his companions, and besides, what did he need them for? — They have nothing — everything eaten, everything drunk — while with us, thank God, there was always a little something to be found — we bought things at the stations. Out of curiosity, Bay Ganyo did not miss the opportunity to try the foreign products:
— What's this, is it grapes? Bravo! Look! Come on, give me a little bunch. Mm! Good! Bravo! Curiosity drove him to get acquainted in this way with our snacks, our cognac, our cigarette cases.
— Is this cigarette case made of Caucasian silver? — Bai Ganyo inquired curiously, seeing one of us preparing to light up.
— No, it isn't, it's of Viennese make! — the owner replied.
— Is that so? Let me see it. Tsk... tsk... tsk! Look! There's tobacco too, Bulgarian, right? Bravo! Wait, let me roll a cigarette. I have cigarette papers, if you need any — I'm right here!

That he was here, we felt it quite a bit: both by the smell of his boots, and by the specific aroma of his sweaty body, and by his aggressive movement toward occupying the entire sofa. At first he sat on the edge of the sofa, then he began to sit more comfortably, later three of us had to sit on one sofa, and Ivanitsov’s son had to curl up on the edge of the other, so that Bai Ganyo could have the opportunity to take a horizontal position. And he did not miss a single chance. We agreed to test how far Bai Ganyo’s need for comfort could go, and he began, in all sincerity, to provide food for our curiosity:

— Move over a bit toward the edge so I can put my other leg up too. That’s it! Bravo! Ahhh! Damn it! What a pleasure! Just listen to the machine: chug-chug, chug-chug! It’s flying!... I love stretching out like this. It’s cramped over there. And the comrades—simple folk, what is there to talk about with them?... What are you eating there, a pear? Bravo! Let’s see if I can eat a pear while lying down like this. Thank you! Where do you get these things from?
— We’ll buy them — one of us replies, barely containing himself.
— Is that so? Bravo! — he approves with a mouth full of the juicy pear. — I love pears.

Bai Ganyo, lulled by the monotonous rhythm of the locomotive, began to doze. I was thinking what, what trick we could play on him. Finally, a brilliant idea struck me. I signaled to my companions beforehand and said:
— Let's make some coffee, gentlemen. Pass the spirit and the burner.
— Coffee? — shouted Bay Ganyo and jumped up from the sofa as if stung. — You bet!
— What coffee are we going to make, there is no water — Ivanitso's son spoke up, artistically feigning.
— Water? — shouted Bai Ganyo in the same voice. — Just ask me for water. Right away! — And he flew out of the compartment.

We were dying of laughter. Ivanitso’s son stretched out and took up the whole sofa. Bay Ganyo returned and was huffing more than was necessary. He had to show us what labor and hardship he had endured for our sake. In his hand, a small pitcher.

— Here, I found it, did you see? I scoured all the carriages! Finally, I saw a pitcher, I grabbed it instantly, and a woman shouted at me: “Hey, give the water here, it’s for my child.” What lie should I tell, what lie should I tell, then it occurred to me: “Excuse me, madam, someone over there has fainted.” “Is that so,” she says. “Yes.” “Well, then take him the water quickly and bring the little pitcher back.” Foolish woman!... Phew! I’m all in a sweat. Now, let’s have some coffee!
— Aren't you ashamed, sir! — said one of the comrades reproachfully, who could no longer contain his indignation.

Bay Ganyo looked at him with a strained face, trying to portray his sincere astonishment as vividly as possible; then, quite unexpectedly, he said:
— It crossed my mind that the whole thing was a setup, but oh well, I said to myself. Well then, give me at least a cigarette and a little cognac.

We gave him a cigarette and some cognac, and he went back to his compartment, to the simple folk. — "What absolute fools these educated ones are," Bay Ganyo's voice was heard a moment later from the neighboring compartment; — "I don't know how they tolerate such people in office. But just you wait, your Bay Ganyo will return to Bulgaria, and then we'll see who's who."

We were approaching the Czech border. Traveling with us were also the commissioners sent by the government to learn how to organize an exhibition, so that they could organize the one in Plovdiv as well. One of them pinned small Bulgarian tricolors on the chests of all the passengers. Along the way, a rumor spread that we would be welcomed ceremoniously both at the border and in Prague; therefore, we were prepared for the meeting—but what we saw in reality surpassed all our expectations.

Here is the border station; the locomotive is already whistling. We see, from the left and right of the railway, crowds of people flocking toward the station. It was drizzling, and the running men, women, and children were carrying open umbrellas. We stopped. The platform was packed with people. Immediately, a band struck up “Shumi Maritsa.” A choir then sang “Kde domov muj” to the infinite pleasure of us all, and especially of Bay Ganyo, who praised the Czech people among us for having learned the tune of the Bulgarian folk song “Where is my kin” quite well, except that they pronounced the words a bit unclearly, so it wasn't very easy to understand.

Blood rushes to my head with shame when I remember the behavior we exhibited during that first meeting. Imagine, gentlemen: the whole town had gathered, people had come from the villages to welcome their Bulgarian brothers, they had brought music, a choir had come, a crowd of girls had lined up with bouquets in hand, waiting for the brothers to get off the train to welcome them, to greet them with words, with songs, with music, with bouquets; but the "brothers" just stuck their heads out of the windows and stared! Believe me, believe me, gentlemen! The windows of the carriages, you know, are narrow; one stuck his head out, another huddled over his shoulder, a third poked out from below only half a distorted face with one eye, and they stared! — It’s enough to make you melt away! Oh, if only there were a snapshot! — The welcomers were stunned. They didn't know what to do either — where to put the bouquets! The music stopped, the choir stopped too, and there followed silence and mutual staring.

At one point Bay Ganyo got off the carriage. All the Czechs fixed their eyes on him and made way for him to pass, and he passed... My God! How importantly Bay Ganyo passed amidst hundreds of eyes and hands that were holding out bouquets to him. He set off with a full hand and twirled his left mustache upward, stuck out his elbows, coughed deeply, and looked with one eye at the young lady who had held her bouquet almost under his nose; he looked at her and wiggled the fingers of his left hand, turned upward, as if he wanted to say: “Are you welcoming me, girl, are you welcoming me? You’re doing well, keep welcoming, I like it” — and he went on his way without deigning to honor her by accepting her bouquet. The girl sheepishly pulled back her hand. After a while Bay Ganyo appeared, not quite gracefully buttoning a part of his attire. Again they made way for him, again he twirled his left mustache, again he coughed, blew his nose with his fingers, and climbed into the carriage. The locomotive whistled and we set off.

Lest any of you think that I am exaggerating, that I am intentionally embellishing my story to caricature Bai Ganyo, I will tell you that, on the contrary, I am omitting certain things, because even now my heart tightens when I recall them. For example, I kept silent at the very beginning about what a sight our train presented as early as the second day of our journey. Didn't I mention to you that our tourists had dragged along their infants as well; setting aside the crying and screaming, I will tell you that the toilets had been turned into laundries, where they washed the children's soiled little shirts and pants, and the corridors of the carriages were turned into drying rooms for this laundry: they stretched out ropes and hung the not-quite-washed pants: they replaced the flags with which we were supposed to decorate our train; instead of the tricolor—white, green, and red—with us, a multitude of bicolors—white and yellow—shone in the sun. These charms adorned our train even when we stopped at the stations in Bohemia and the people welcomed us with music, songs, bouquets, and welcoming speeches from mayors and other representatives. These yellow-and-white flags fluttered on the ropes even when our leader, Mr. Vasilaki, deafened the Czech listeners with his loud, sentimental speeches, and when Mr. Petko tickled the national pride of the brotherly Czech people at every station with his oratorical words, from which those standing further away could clearly hear only the words: “Brothers! Jan Hus... Oh! Jan Hus, brothers!”, and when Bai Ganyo, indignant that the speeches did not mention our historical giants, poked a teacher in the ribs with the words: “Teacher, you say something too, man, let's show them who we are, now is the time, say something about either Filip Totyu or Krum the Terrible, or sing a song...” And the bicolor flags kept on fluttering!...

Our entire journey from the Czech border to Prague was one triumphal procession; whether past towns, or villages, or through fields—wherever our train passed, hats flew into the air and an endless “nazdar!” rent the air.

I noticed a female worker in the field who, seeing that the men were waving and throwing their hats, waved and waved her hands, then went and untied the kerchief from her head, whirled it in the air, and shrieked: “Nazdaar!” Another thing: we were passing by a town (I don’t remember what it was called, and how could one remember, we were stunned then), people in the streets, people at the windows, on the trees, on the fences, and even on the eaves. So in this town, I remember, I noticed in one place, a new house was being built, almost finished, and the beams of the roof were laid out, at the top of the roof a long pole was stuck, decorated with greenery, and at its tip a flag (just like with us, when they build houses): several workers from above, seeing that along the whole street from all the floors people were waving kerchiefs and shouting “nazdaar!”, ran along the beams toward the top of the roof, grabbed the pole with the flag and pulled to take it out to salute us, but, it seemed, it was firmly fixed — they couldn’t pull it out, but they shook it at the base enough so that it could wave with a small amplitude left and right. These two instances — with the workers in the field and the masons on the roof — moved me to the highest degree. This was not like ours: “The entire intelligentsia rent the air with frenetic hurrahs,” “Today the whole nation rejoices...”

We arrived at the station in Prague. On the platform, we did not notice many people; there were only official greeters: the deputy mayor, if I am not mistaken, and members of the exhibition committee. This meeting seemed dull to me; we had grown accustomed to triumph! But as it turned out, there was a reason for it; the people, being more organized, know that when 160 people get off the train, if there is a crowd on the platform, they will get mixed up and confused: it would become a mess of guests, hosts, and luggage, so they left the platform empty and only a committee appeared to meet us. Greetings and speeches began again, on one side: “Bratri...! Bulhari...! Veliky slovansky... Cyrila Metodej,” on the other side: “Bratri, my jsme prsli poucit se u velkeho ceskeho naroda!”... on a third side: “Brothers! The great Jan Hus!... Yes, brothers, Jan Hus is great!” And Bay Ganyo, for his part, dissatisfied that they mentioned only Cyril and Methodius, nudged the teacher again: “You say something too, teacher, don't we have plenty of our own? Tell them about Asparuh, or go ahead and blow the kaval—now is the time!...”

Here they told us that we would all go to the city club "Meshtanska Beseda," and from there we would be assigned to our lodgings. They arranged for our luggage to be brought there. We set off. From the platform, we entered the station hall, and what a sight! People! Swarming with people! Literally, there wasn't even room to drop an egg. In the middle, there was a single path, just wide enough for us to pass through. On either side stood rows of ladies with bouquets. Everyone was dressed in their holiday best. Then a thunderous "Nazdar!" rang out, and they began handing us bouquets and showering us with flowers. When we stepped out onto the street and looked—Lord!—as far as the eye could see, they had left only a narrow path for us, while everything else was packed with people. There were rows of ladies again, and more shouts of "Nazdaaar! Nazdaaar! Hurrah!"—and another hail of bouquets. A royal welcome!... Amidst the shouts and the flowers, we climbed into carriages and set off. Now, as for how gracefully we were seated and settled with our families and infants—I leave that to your imagination! We were absolutely stunned by this unexpected, grand reception! We tipped our hats left and right; then we thought to take them off entirely (when it comes to being quick-witted, oh, we were very quick-witted indeed! We know how to handle these things, the etiquette!). A smile was frozen on my convulsively trembling lips, and it felt as if I wanted to laugh, to cry, and to sink into the ground all at once!

We arrived at "Měšťanská beseda" and took the tables in the garden. We were waiting for our luggage to arrive and for us to be assigned to lodgings. Several carriage drivers waited, poor things, for a whole hour around the gates to be paid, but many of our tourists did not find it necessary to pay. "Big deal," Bay Ganyo would say, "what does it cost them to pay for our carriages? After all—we are Slavs! Let them show their Slavdom here, come on! Of course! Everything for free! With money, even an old woman knows how! Just a bare—nazdar"...

The luggage arrived and they began sending us to our lodgings. People had taken care to find us rooms. I will not tell you about the quarrels with the coachmen, with the waiters in the club, with the organizers about the delays or the mistaken swapping of luggage, about the dissatisfactions with the lodgings, about the haggling and other such things. Let us transport ourselves with you for a minute into our room (do not be afraid, madam). The four of us settled into a large room. We had all the comforts. Our room looked out onto the courtyard... On the opposite side, the same number of floors rose up. At one point the maid who was attending to us, Anushka, as she was taking down the flower pots from the windows so she could close them, suddenly turned to me and asked me embarrassedly, pointing with her eyes toward the windows opposite:
— Please, sir, is that gentleman also a Bulgarian? Look at what he's doing! He's so black! Hairy like some kind of savage! Ha-ha-ha-ha!

I look in the indicated direction and what do I see? Bay Ganyo, with open windows, without drawing the curtains or the blinds, having freed himself from his upper garments, and at the moment I looked, he was grinning at our maid and stroking his hairy chest; apparently, he wanted to captivate her with this.

In the local newspapers that same day, greetings appeared for the dear (they were right) guests — *bratri Bulhari*. The program was also printed, according to which we were to visit the exhibition and the landmarks of the city of Prague. They printed reports of our visits: where we had gone, how we had been received, how they had welcomed us, and what we had answered them. The name of our leader, Mr. Vasilaki, resounded; he earned this attention with his countless speeches. And to tell the truth, say what you will, but if it hadn't been for Mr. Vasilaki to pull the wool over their eyes a bit, we would have failed completely.

At the entrance of the exhibition, we were met by members of the committee. And again, speeches about the *cesheho naroda*, about the *bulharskeho naroda*. Here, you see, they didn't make the mistake of welcoming us as Serbs, a mistake which, they say, occurred at the entrance of the Plovdiv Exhibition: the people of Sliven and Yambol were in constant antagonism—whether out of envy, or rivalry, who knows why. The people of Sliven appeared before the entrance of the Plovdiv Exhibition, and one of the committee members gave them a speech, thinking they were the people of Yambol, and praised them, and praised them: "The brave Yambolians, the glorious Yambolians!" And the Slivenites were sweating, coughing into their palms, blinking... Quite a picture!...

We entered the exhibition. One of the committee led us to make a quick general overview of the main departments. And who was he leading? — Our tourists — real Englishmen!... Once those people of yours entered the botanical department — there was no coming out!
— Ivancho, Ivancho, come, come here, look at the tulip, how big it is! Do you remember, your aunt has a tulip like that! — one calls out from one side.
— Mariyka, Mariyka, come, come here, look, a mimosa, this is a mimosa, do you see? Do you remember in the little atlas that I bought for you for Easter? — shouts another from the other side.
— Look, basil! Tsk... tsk... tsk... Even the Czechs have basil, bravo! — a third one says, and they rush to look at the basil.
— Hey, I don't see any geranium here — Bay Ganyo speaks up in a dissatisfied voice, — they're a sorry lot if they don't have geranium! Ah, back home! In the Balkans! Eh, damn it all!
And the committee member meanwhile was on pins and needles! They were waiting for the dear guests to finish their talk!...

I could not restrain myself; I left the botanical department and went to gawk around the other pavilions. In my absence, the distinguished guests were photographed, and the next day, the whole group appeared in an illustrated newspaper.

They took us to Hradčany, where the palaces of the Czech kings are located. They showed us various historical nooks: the small room where the council met and the start of the Thirty Years' War was decided; the window through which the Czech patriots were thrown into the abyss. They took us to the old town hall, to the old and the new museum. They gave an opera in our honor at the Národní divadlo, they gave a soirée at the “Měšťanská beseda.” We went to Mr. Náprstek’s, a highly respected citizen, once compromised before the Austrian government, fled to America, built a fortune there, returned to Prague and now, surrounded by honors and respect, occupies himself with philanthropy. He has his own museum and library. The host welcomed us with all the cordiality and hospitality of a Slav. Here the most heartfelt speeches were delivered. In one of the rooms there was a thick book in which visitors recorded their names. At one point, when many had crowded around the book and everyone was hurrying to grab the pen and immortalize their name, Bay Ganyo pulled me by the sleeve and impatiently asked me:
— Hey, what are they signing up for there?

I, knowing in advance that no pretext for signing would satisfy Bai Ganyo if nothing for the sake of appearances resulted from it, told him jokingly: whoever does not wish to tour the antiquities of Prague any further may sign this book and have lunch at pan Naprstek’s.

— Is that so? — cried Bay Ganyo. — To hell with their antiquities, give me the pen! Give it, man, give me the pen quickly! Can't it be done with a pencil? Give it, give it, I'm in a hurry! — and he began to elbow his way toward the table on which the large book lay. They stepped on each other, they jostled with one another, they began to snatch the pen from each other, they dripped ink on the book, and finally, the trembling, hairy, and sweaty hand of Bay Ganyo adorned one of the pages with two resonant words: Ganyo Balkanski
Tsvyatko told us that he does not wish to continue his story.
— Tell us something about the party. Didn't you say they gave a party in honor of the Bulgarians? — one of the group spoke up.

— I didn't go to that party. Bay Ganyo did. A propos, on that day I went with Bay Ganyo to a barbershop. He intended to captivate the Czech ladies that evening and was taking all sorts of preliminary measures to appear in all his splendor: he bought himself a tie, cleaned his medal (for what did you think of your Bay Ganyo!) and we went to the barbershop, because his hair and beard were quite overgrown. He sat in the chair. The barber carefully wrapped him up and began his work. We were delayed here for almost a whole hour. It was not so easy to please Bay Ganyo.

— Here, here; tell him here — and Bay Ganyo points to his neck — to smooth it out here, to scrape a bit with the razor. And tell him to keep his eyes open, not to cut any little pimple, or the devils will take him.
The barber sees through the mirror the angry expression of Bai Ganyo’s sweaty face and looks at me in bewilderment.

— What is the gentleman saying? — he asked me humbly, thinking that he had committed some error against Bay Ganyo’s taste. — You tell him to set the talk aside now — Bay Ganyo turns to me, and in such a tone as if he had hired me as an interpreter. — Tell him to leave me a goatee and let him make it a bit sharper, like Napoleon’s, do you understand? And let him comb the mustache so they puff up, like — he, he! — the Italian king’s, hi-hi-hi! Have you seen him pictured? Make them like that! Tell him, then!

I did not have the courage to translate literally Bay Ganyo’s modest wish; it would have put the barber in a great predicament: is it an easy task, with the help of a razor and a comb, to make someone look like both Napoleon III and Humbert! And whom?

The hairdressing was finished. Bay Ganyo pulled out his purse, wound it around the string, opened it, reached to the bottom, scooped up a handful of coins, turned his back to us, rummaged and rummaged through the coins, picked one out and handed it to the barber, but handed it in such a way as if he wanted to say: “There, take it, oh well, let it go.” The coin was twenty kreuzers. But realizing he might have made a mistake, and not wanting to be thought a fool, he gestured with his fingers toward the barber, as if to say “give me change.” In an instant, the barber opened the drawer, threw the coin inside, picked out two ten-kreuzer coins, slammed them angrily onto the marble table, and disappeared through an inner door. The coins rolled onto the floor. For a moment, Bay Ganyo seemed startled, somewhat puzzled, but I couldn’t quite catch that impression before he bent down, gathered the money, and said:
— Angry Petko—his bag is empty! Come on, forget them! All they know is how to fleece you! Don't I know them! Slavs!... Rubbish!...
